cells.tense: Right now something is arriving, and you are meeting it before you have decided what it is or what it should become.
cells.ask: Before you sort the day, name one thing you're carrying that hasn't happened yet — say what it is, not what it should be.
cells.core:
You're at the edge of something that hasn't taken shape, and you're not rushing it into one. That's not indecision. To be present before the choice gets made, with the whole thing still open, is the harder posture and you're in it.

On a good day you can feel a direction forming without grabbing it. Nothing needs to be settled this minute for you to move. You let what shows up show itself first, and you act from what's actually there rather than the plan you brought. Most people arrive already finished, already knowing what the room will be. You come in with the room still open, and what's real gets a chance to come through.
cells.sheetLine: You meet what's arriving before you decide what it should be.
cells.verb: standing at the open door of what has not yet become
cells.place: the threshold where what is arriving meets what can receive it

cells.tense: Ahead of you there is a version of this where everything finally fits, and you are living in that version instead of the one you're in.
cells.ask: Pick the possibility you keep circling and give it one concrete hour today — small enough to actually do.
cells.core:
You're in what might happen more than in what is. Every open path gets held next to every other open path, and that puts the whole day into comparison. The options stay bright because you keep setting none of them down.

When one of them does land, something else is happening. You feel a version gaining a little weight, and you follow the weight instead of re-checking the field. The other paths stay there without running the day. Keeping them all open protects the feeling of not being wrong yet, and it also keeps you from finding out which one was the one.
cells.sheetLine: You keep every door open and haven't walked through any of them.
cells.verb: standing at the open door of what has not yet become
cells.place: the threshold where what is arriving meets what can receive it

cells.tense: You are meeting what arrives from behind a door that closed, giving each moment less of yourself than you have to give.
cells.ask: Tell one person something you've wanted, before you've decided whether you're allowed to want it.
cells.core:
You still read what's coming. You just don't step toward it. You watch from where you are and call it being careful; the watching has become the whole posture, and what's here gets a measured answer instead of a real one.

On a good day something new gets an unfiltered response from you — wanted or not, right or not. The first move doesn't need to be good. If the read is wrong and nothing much is arriving, the ask still shows you what you've been holding back, and that's its own information. You aren't empty. There's a way through that's still yours, and it's smaller than the whole thing looks from here.
cells.sheetLine: You stay behind the doorway, answering less than what's here.
cells.verb: standing at the open door of what has not yet become
cells.place: the threshold where what is arriving meets what can receive it

cells.tense: You are already answering what arrives, but you call those answers the situation instead of your own moves, so the options stay invisible to you.
cells.ask: When you feel pushed toward something today, stop once — do what you'd do if nobody were steering.
cells.core:
Things show up and you move, and afterward it looks like the day decided. But you're the one reading what came in and picking how to meet it. That part runs in you without a marker on it, so the doors look gone when they're only unwitnessed.

On a good day the second before the answer has a little air in it. You notice you're about to move and you see the move as a move. That isn't a flaw to fix. It's how attention has been spent, and attention can be spent differently starting with the next time something arrives. You're already in the middle of meeting this.
cells.sheetLine: You're already answering what arrives — the door is you, not the room.

attempts.check: The claim I'm making is that the person already knows what wants to arrive and only needs to claim that knowing — the record supports what's arriving but not that they've already perceived it correctly. A reader could say the real issue is exterior: nothing is arriving, the door is closed from the other side. The ask survives being wrong because it only asks the person to look at what they've been calling blocked, which teaches them something either way. The sentence that serves me is the one that makes 'possibility' sound like a gift rather than a pressure — I've kept it plain.
